content: When designing interventions, it is essential to consider the criteria and questions outlined above to guide their prioritization. Once interventions are identified, these criteria can further inform their ranking and implementation. Modeling the Impact of Tuberculosis (TB): Impact modeling can estimate and compare the potential health and non-health effects (such as equity, financial protection, and poverty reduction) of implementing specific intervention scenarios. When used, modeling should adhere to established principles and best practices for country-level modeling. The absence of local data should not diminish the prioritization of interventions, as evidence from other settings can also be considered to assess potential impacts. A formal modeling exercise is not always required to address all TB policy and program strategy questions. Allocative efficiency modeling, for example, focuses on maximizing health impact among competing priorities within a given budget. This involves costing identified interventions and comparing their cost-effectiveness to determine the package of interventions that will yield the greatest overall health benefits. Example of Feasibility and Impact Assessment for TB Diagnostics: To improve access to TB diagnostic services, objectives include: Increasing the TB case detection rate by raising the percentage of newly notified patients diagnosed using a WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic test (WRD) from 38% in 2017 to 70% in 2023. Expanding drug susceptibility testing (DST) coverage to all previously treated TB patients (from 75% to 100%) and to 80% of newly diagnosed cases with bacteriological confirmation. Increasing the proportion of sites using WRDs with established connectivity systems for electronic reporting to clinicians and digital reporting systems (from 20% to 50%). Proposed Actions: 1. Integrated Sample Referral Systems: Establish policies and implementation frameworks across diseases and partners. Implement electronic tracking systems. 2. Optimize Diagnostic Device Placement and Network Structure: Conduct diagnostic network optimization analyses. Engage private sector laboratories and providers. 3. Adopt New WHO-Recommended Tools and Approaches: Link GeneXpert laboratory information systems (LIMS) to national health information systems like TIBU and DHIS. Incorporate tools for pediatric TB, sequencing, Omni, and LAM testing. 4. Remove Cost Barriers to TB Diagnosis: Negotiate diagnostic pricing for the private sector. Partner with the Ministry of Health (MOH) and other organizations. Setting Epidemiological Targets: A critical step in planning is estimating the target population for each intervention. Coverage targets influence the scale, scope, and cost of the plan. Target setting should consider factors such as TB epidemiology, demographics, economic performance, political developments, and the relative significance of TB compared to other health priorities. There is no standard formula for setting targets; they should be determined by stakeholders based on the country context and available information. Projections of TB Notifications: Future TB notification targets should primarily rely on recent notification trends rather than incidence estimates. For example, if a country notified 1,000 TB cases last year, projections for this year may assume a similar number unless specific drivers (e.g., improved detection rates or service disruptions) are anticipated to cause changes. Dynamic models can help predict the short-term impact of TB service disruptions, such as those caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, natural disasters, or conflicts. Operational Planning: Activities and sub-activities under each intervention should be detailed to guide practitioners at all levels of the health system. This includes identifying required inputs, specifying and quantifying target populations, and listing resources needed (financial, technical, and human). Operational plans should be flexible and responsive, with annual and mid-term reviews to refine planning based on lessons learned and changes in the operational environment. Contingency Planning for Emergencies: In the post-acute phase, efforts should focus on rehabilitating infrastructure, tracing patients with interrupted treatment, and adapting national TB plans to the new context. Monitoring, Evaluation, and Review: The NSP should include metrics and activities to monitor progress, evaluate performance, and review implementation. This involves tracking the implementation of activities, assessing progress toward goals and objectives, addressing inequities in service access, and ensuring transparency and accountability. Surveillance systems should be maintained and strengthened to provide quality data for decision-making and quality improvement processes. Considerations for Protracted Crises: In prolonged emergencies, maintaining leadership of the National TB Program (NTP) and strengthening program capacities at national and subnational levels are critical. Mapping and identifying affected populations and ensuring the inclusion of TB services in broader health cluster responses are essential for sustaining TB care and prevention efforts.
